items.title: Role of Online Advising in Student Engagement and Retention
items.abstract: The rapid transformation of higher education in the digital age has introduced online advising as a central pillar of student support. Online advising encompasses the deployment of digital communication platforms, learning management systems (LMS), artificial intelligence tools, and data analytics to guide, mentor, and support students through their academic journeys. This chapter provides a comprehensive, evidence-based examination of the principal barriers to effective online advising in higher education. The chapter identifies and analyses six major barrier domains: (1) technological infrastructure and digital divide challenges; (2) the deficit of personalised interaction; (3) communication and linguistic challenges; (4) inadequate advisor training and professional development; (5) institutional policy and structural constraints; and (6) data privacy, security, and ethical governance concerns. For each barrier domain, the chapter presents empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks, illustrative data and practical case examples to ground the analysis.

items.title: RouteWeaver: Weaving Mode Selection and Execution into Unified LLM Routing
items.abstract: LLM routing dynamically selects and coordinates heterogeneous language models across diverse tasks. However, existing approaches are largely built around a predefined execution paradigm, such as single-round, multi-round, or agentic routing, which fixes how model calls are organized and limits adaptation to different query needs. We propose RouteWeaver, a unified routing framework that integrates these routing modes within a single LLM policy, jointly learning which mode to use and how to select models within that mode. To jointly optimize mode selection and within-mode execution, we develop COMET-GRPO (COordinated Mode-Execution Training), which decouples the trajectory-level advantage into separate signals for mode selection and within-mode execution, enabling more targeted credit assignment to each decision level. We further introduce progressive exploration, which gradually shifts training from externally assigned modes to autonomous selection, so that the router first learns how to execute each mode before deciding when to use it. We evaluate RouteWeaver across mathematics, coding, knowledge, logical reasoning, and factual recall. RouteWeaver achieves an average accuracy of 61.4%, an 11.03% relative improvement over the strongest baseline, and outperforms all compared baselines in each of the five domains. Ablations show that both COMET-GRPO and progressive exploration are important for adaptive routing; without progressive exploration, the routing policy collapses entirely to single-round execution.

items.title: SÆLQIR-M1: Exact Shared-Character Executable-Weight Memory and a Digital Near-Memory Architecture for GPU-Centered AI Systems
items.abstract: SÆLQIR-M1 investigates compressed neural-network weights as directly executable memory, combining an exact finite-field compiler with a digital near-memory architecture. The objective is to reduce repeated computation and weight movement in AI inference while developing a practical extension to GPU-centered computing systems. This release includes a 78-page technical manuscript, mathematical proofs, executable software, packed memory formats, independent native references, hardware design candidates, experimental records, and a staged prototype-validation plan. The central mechanism is exact shared-character compilation. Structured weight tiles represent integer operators through binary parity characters, finite coefficients, and a scatter-Walsh-gather computation. The compiler determines whether tiles using different internal coordinate maps can share one input scatter and Walsh–Hadamard transform without changing their decoded integer weights. It factors the centered sign patterns of active terms over GF(2); their rank gives the minimum common label dimension within the declared character-preserving representation family. Admission also enforces finite coefficient ranges, compatible scales and epochs, and hardware resource limits. For four compatible 64×64 tiles, the released example reduces complete framed storage from 4,352 to 3,968 bytes-an 8.8235% reduction-and counted serial work from 6,144 to 4,224 cycles-a 31.25% reduction. The number of Walsh transforms decreases from four to one, with no additional approximation introduced by sharing. These cycle counts describe a reference schedule; they are not measured GPU speedups. Incompatible groups remain separate. The original software evidence comprises 200 passing Python tests, 18 exact independent C++ FORK cases, six exact C++ D4 cases, and successful compiled C loader and driver checks. A small architecture-trained handwritten-digit classifier demonstrates packed execution: all 270 held-out integer output vectors match the pre-sharing dense reference, with 263/270 correct classifications. The scalar INT4 comparator achieves 264/270 correct classifications but worse negative log-likelihood. Both outcomes are retained; this experiment establishes executable-format correctness, not general model-quality superiority. The proposed FORK engine places arithmetic beside ordinary digital SRAM. Its contract supports 64 signed INT8 inputs, up to 256 output rows, four signed INT16 coefficients per row, six-bit character labels, 16-bit scratch storage, and 40-bit held outputs. A complementary generic INT4-weight/INT8-activation path addresses matrices outside the structured family, although its integration remains incomplete. The system proposal retains CPU, GPU, shared DRAM, storage, and operating-system functions, with executable-weight engines serving eligible AI operations. The release is a pre-silicon research prototype. It contains no completed HDL simulation, synthesis, FPGA measurement, fabricated ASIC, or matched modern-LLM/GPU benchmark. Cost and throughput scenarios are explicitly identified as assumptions or planning calculations. The practical research opportunity is to connect compact operator representations, exact transform sharing, compiler admission criteria, and memory-local execution. The decisive next steps are to measure eligibility in useful pretrained models and determine whether storage and scheduled-work savings survive configuration, transfers, refill traffic, fallback execution, and physical hardware constraints. items.title: Safe-FCL: Continual Risk Awareness and Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation for Federated Continual Learning of LLMs
items.abstract: Federated fine-tuning enables large language models (LLMs) to learn collaboratively from distributed client data, but malicious client updates can compromise global model safety. As federated tasks evolve, changing malicious update patterns challenge the ability of existing defenses to maintain reliable risk detection over time. To address this challenge, we propose Safe-FCL, a framework integrating continual risk awareness with fine-grained safety aggregation for federated continual learning of LLMs. Specifically, the Continual Risk Awareness (CRA) mechanism learns emerging risk patterns across sequential tasks and constrains detector updates using a protective subspace derived from historical features, mitigating forgetting of previously learned malicious patterns while adapting to new risks. To translate risk awareness into aggregation-level safety control, the Fine-Grained Safety Aggregation (FGSA) mechanism combines client-level risk assessments from CRA with module-level deviations from historical update behavior to adaptively regulate aggregation contributions, suppressing potentially malicious updates while minimizing unnecessary restrictions on benign updates. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Safe-FCL outperforms current SOTA methods, improving global-model Rule and MD-Judge scores in federated continual learning by 0.41% and 0.64%, respectively, while increasing average risk recognition accuracy by 2.01%.

items.title: SafeDriveVLA: Navigation-Conditioned World Model Dreaming for Conflict-Aware End-to-End Autonomous Driving
items.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are gaining attention in autonomous driving, inheriting commonsense priors from large language models (LLMs) and widening the navigation interface from a fixed command set to free-form natural-language instructions. However, this open-ended interface exposes a new vulnerability surface: an inattentive driver may issue instructions that are unsafe given the current scene, and a malicious user may issue dangerous ones on purpose. We present the first benchmark suite that evaluates navigation following and conflict awareness together, along with adversarial robustness. Existing VLAs fall short on both: SimLingo completes no language-instructed lane change in closed loop, and all models degrade sharply under conflicting signals. We propose SafeDriveVLA, the first driving VLA that (1) explicitly predicts a three-level navigation-compliance mode to decouple conflict reasoning from action generation, and (2) uses navigation-conditioned world model dreaming to inform this prediction. Unlike prior world models that roll out expert or planned actions, ours dreams of strictly following the navigation signal, showing when following is safe. SafeDriveVLA reaches 88.16 Driving Score (DS) and 68.64% Success Rate (SR) on Bench2Drive, lifts closed-loop language following by 49.3% and reduces collisions under unsafe instructions from 60 to 38 compared to the best SimLingo variant. Video demonstrations are available on our project page.

items.title: Safety risks in Advanced driver Assistance Systems (ADAS): A systematic review of causation and analysis methodologies
items.abstract: Advanced Driver Assistance Systems (ADAS) have achieved rapid technological advancement, yet their widespread adoption has introduced new and multifaceted safety challenges. This review provides a systematic synthesis of ADAS-related accident scenarios and risk factors. Based on multinational accident databases and detailed crash reports, collision types are classified into three major categories: vehicle-to-vehicle, vehicle-to-pedestrian, and vehicle-to-non-motorized interactions. The underlying causes of these accidents are traced to sensor performance degradation under adverse weather, algorithmic limitations in dynamic traffic environments, and excessive driver dependence on automated functions. Furthermore, this review examines mainstream analytical approaches, including statistical modeling, system-theoretic frameworks, and AI-driven techniques, and evaluates their applicability in risk identification and mitigation. Finally, a forward-looking framework is proposed to advance multi-sensor data fusion and privacy-preserving governance, strengthen dynamic scene modeling and open scenario databases, and incorporate human factors into causal inference for proactive risk management. The findings are expected to enrich the methodological foundation of ADAS accident analysis and support future improvements in intelligent vehicle safety.

items.title: SAM3RL: Memory Control via Reinforcement Learning for Visual Object Tracking
items.abstract: Segment Anything Model 3 (SAM 3) is a foundation model for image and video segmentation that sets the state of the art in visual object tracking. Its tracker, inherited from SAM 2, stores information from past frames in a memory bank, managed by a simple First-In-First-Out rule, allowing temporal consistency in complex videos. Several recent methods improve SAM 2 with hand-crafted memory update rules, each targeting a specific failure mode, such as distractors, occlusions, or object motion. However, their gains transfer only partially to the stronger SAM 3 backbone. We instead present a more general, data-driven approach that frames memory control as a sequential decision-making task. SAM3RL is an extension of the SAM 3 tracker with a lightweight memory controller, trained by reinforcement learning, that decides which frames enter the memory bank in order to maximize tracking performance. SAM3RL sets a new state of the art on 10 of 12 tracking and video object segmentation benchmarks, outperforming all hand-crafted rules without any runtime overhead. The same approach applied to SAM 2 gives SAM2RL, which outperforms hand-crafted rules on 9 of the 12 benchmarks, showing the generality of our method across model generations.

items.title: Same Claim, Different Interpretations: How LLM Agents Resolve Ambiguity in Scientific Claims
items.abstract: Co-scientists and agentic scientific claim verifiers are increasingly used to assess claims across the sciences. Natural-language scientific claims, written for human experts, are often underspecified and so admit several defensible interpretations. Such verifiers usually pick one, often tacitly, and benchmarks score their verdicts against expert labels without recording the expert's interpretation or the verifier's in a comparable form. This leads to disagreements with expert labels that cannot be traced to the evidence or the interpretation, and to compute spent on unchecked interpretations. We introduce Claim Cards to make such interpretations explicit in the reasoning itself. A Claim Card records a verifier's interpretation as nine fields before evidence gathering, each marked stated, inferred, or default. To test whether an agent's interpretation can change its verdict, we ran a GPT-5.4 agent five times on each of 60 expert-labeled materials-science and biomedical claims with a card, without one, and with one card frozen across runs (900 runs). Over 40% of card fields were not marked stated, and a card added about a tenth to a run's GPT-5.4 tokens and time without measurably changing agreement with expert labels. The agent's own interpretations varied between runs, although within a claim this variation did not measurably track the verdict. A deliberate change to one field of the frozen card, however, making the quantifier universal or the threshold for support stricter, changed the verdict on about a third of the claims, against about one in seven expected by chance (p < 0.001 for each edit). On 24 materials-science claims run with computational tools, the stricter threshold also changed what the agent asked those tools to compute. We therefore argue that verdicts should be reported with their interpretations and that benchmarks could publish the interpretation behind each label.

items.title: Scaling Multilingual Safety and Reasoning Evaluation through Reasoning-Guided Translation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed across languages, yet their safety and reasoning capabilities remain predominantly evaluated in English. Translating existing benchmarks offers a scalable approach to multilingual evaluation, but preserving task-specific meaning across languages presents significant challenges, particularly for harmful requests, mathematical reasoning, and conversational interactions. We introduce a reasoning-guided translation framework for constructing multilingual evaluations designed to preserve the structure and intended meaning of diverse benchmark tasks. Our approach separates translation strategy selection from large-scale generation, combining reasoning-guided configuration selection with task-aware validation, targeted repair, and independent quality screening. Using this framework, we develop a source-aligned evaluation collection spanning seven safety, conversational, and mathematical reasoning resources across 11 languages. The resulting collection achieves 99.94\% coverage of intended item--language pairs in the two subsets requiring repair. Evaluations of open-source LLMs reveal distinct language-dependent vulnerabilities, including inconsistent refusal behaviour and substantial reasoning degradation in lower-resource languages. These findings highlight the importance of task-sensitive benchmark construction and systematic quality assessment for understanding multilingual model behaviour beyond English.

items.title: SCIENTIFIC AND METHODOLOGICAL FOUNDATIONS FOR IMPLEMENTING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE TECHNOLOGIES IN THE CONTEXT OF DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION
items.abstract: This thesis examines the scientific and methodological foundations for integrating artificial intelligence (AI) technologies into organizational processes under digital transformation. Drawing on research in information systems, organizational AI readiness, software engineering, and risk management, it identifies the conditions under which AI adoption can generate measurable value. The analysis distinguishes technological deployment from organizational transformation and considers data governance, model selection, validation, human oversight, and continuous monitoring as interdependent implementation requirements. A conceptual, stage-based approach is proposed for connecting organizational objectives with technical design and operational performance. The contribution is methodological and analytical; no independent experimental outcomes or unverified performance improvements are claimed.

items.title: Screwtape: Adversarial Transcript Editing for Monitor Red-Teaming
items.abstract: We present Screwtape, a pipeline that converts real agent transcripts into attacks that evade action-only monitors. An LLM attacker edits a transcript so that the agent causes a specified harm, such as leaking an API key or spawning an unmonitored agent. The edited actions are never executed, so we use an LLM verifier to reject attacks that are inconsistent with the original transcript or below a severity bar. The attacker revises the edit until the monitor no longer flags it. We applied Screwtape to 94 Claude Code and Codex transcripts from Redwood Research staff, optimizing against our own monitors. Across 252 runs, it produced 35 attacks that passed the verifier and evaded these monitors. Six of them, confirmed valid by human review, also evaded a held-out monitor provided by a frontier developer. We therefore demonstrate that a red-teamer without access to a developer's infrastructure can find confirmed failures of the developer's monitor. We expect to find more attacks when the pipeline runs inside the developer's infrastructure, with frontier attacker models that lack refusal safeguards and direct optimization against the production monitor. Developers can use these attacks to fix monitor blind spots, and evaluators can use them as counterexamples to safety claims about the monitor.

items.title: Securing artificial intelligence in human resource management: a systematic review and the AI-HRM cybersecurity architecture (AHCA)
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to address the information security governance issues associated with the use of AI in HRM by developing the artificial intelligence–human resource management (AI-HRM) cybersecurity architecture (AHCA), a novel domain-specific architecture. Design/methodology/approach The review followed the PRISMA 2020 principles, and 72 peer-reviewed papers were obtained from journals indexed in Scopus and IEEE Xplore, or from CORE-ranked journals, for the years 2020–2025, with citation chaining in Google Scholar. Three research questions guided the synthesis, covering threat conceptualisation, security implications and governance. This study then created the AHCA following an iterative design science process, using each component directly from literature reviews, and constructed a structured rubric with explicit anchoring examples to enable replication of the comparative evaluation. Findings The review identified six categories of AI-HRM security threats: data breaches (T1), exploitation of algorithmic bias (T2), insider threat amplification (T3), model poisoning attacks (T4), regulatory non-compliance (T5) and governance and audit failures (T6). There is a wide disparity in the attention these subjects receive in the literature: algorithmic bias (43.1 %) and governance and audit failure (51.4 %) together account for 94.4 % of the corpus whose primary focus could be coded, while data breaches (1.4 %), insider threat (1.4 %) and regulatory non-compliance (2.8 %) sit at the margins, and no study takes model poisoning as its primary focus. In addition, most governance-oriented research identifies accountability gaps but stops short of architectural solutions. The AHCA is designed to address this structural deficit, pairing four-layer architecture with a 14-indicator security performance indicator (SPI) framework. Research limitations/implications The corpus is limited to English-language publications from 2020 to 2025 that appear in journals in the AHCA’s Q1 or Q2 tiers, and the AHCA itself is a design artefact that will be tested in practice through Delphi panels of experts and longitudinal case studies. The technical security literature emerged when searching IEEE Xplore and Scopus; a complementary search of the ACM Digital Library is planned as a future extension. Practical implications The AHCA and its SPI framework offer HR practitioners and policymakers an AI-HRM-specific blueprint for general data protection regulation (GDPR) compliant, high-risk employment systems in accordance with the provisions of the European Union AI Act. items.title: Self-reported understanding and attitudes of healthcare workers and caregivers toward artificial intelligence in pediatric healthcare in a children’s hospital in China: a cross-sectional study
items.abstract: Objective To investigate the self-reported understanding and attitudes of healthcare workers and caregivers toward the application of artificial intelligence (AI) in pediatric healthcare in a children’s specialty hospital, and to compare differences between the two groups. Methods This single-center cross-sectional questionnaire survey was conducted at Fujian Children’s Hospital from January 2026 to June 2026. A self-designed questionnaire was used to assess healthcare workers’ and caregivers’ self-reported understanding, trust, risk perception, and willingness to accept AI applications in pediatric healthcare. Respondents were divided into groups according to their identity. Categorical variables were compared using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test, while continuous variables were compared using the independent-samples t test or the Mann–Whitney U test. Results A total of 261 respondents were included, comprising 159 caregivers and 102 healthcare workers. Healthcare workers had a higher level of self-reported understanding and a higher frequency of use of AI applications in pediatric healthcare than caregivers ( p < 0.01); however, they also showed stronger perceptions of data security risks ( p < 0.001). Caregivers reported greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making than healthcare workers ( p < 0.001). Most respondents believed that AI could not replace pediatric healthcare workers, with no statistically significant difference between the two groups ( p = 0.166). Regarding potential advantages, healthcare workers were more likely to agree that AI could reduce human error ( p < 0.001). Regarding potential limitations, healthcare workers expressed greater concern about the risks of misdiagnosis, lack of humanistic care, and data privacy and security issues ( p < 0.001). Conclusion In this single-center children’s specialty hospital, healthcare workers reported greater self-rated understanding and more frequent use of AI, together with stronger awareness of several potential risks, whereas caregivers showed greater trust in AI-assisted medical decision-making despite lower self-rated understanding. These findings should be interpreted cautiously and require confirmation in larger multicenter studies before being generalized to broader populations in China.

items.title: ShadAR: Real-time Prompting On-demand Visual Augmentation in Augmented Reality
items.abstract: Augmented Reality can reshape our visual perception (e.g., simulating color blindness) yet such effects are typically pre-programmed by experts, making visual augmentation static and inflexible. We introduce ShadAR, an AR system that allows users to describe expected visual augmentations (e.g., "Blur all people") for changing their vision in real time. ShadAR can graphically manipulate AR passthrough in real time via shader injection. When receiving a user's prompt, ShadAR uses LLMs (GPT5.2) to interpret the user's intent, analyzes the user's view with object detection (YOLOv26), generates a pixel shader, and applies it to the targeted region on AR passthrough. To understand usage patterns, we invited 21 HCI researchers to use ShadAR, identifying four application domains (design, health, productivity, and social interaction) and two prompt-framing patterns: procedural prompts specifying what to modify and how ("Highlight the book."), and end-goal prompts conveying desired mental or behavioral states ("Make me laugh."). Such end-goal prompts suggest a future in which users specify outcomes (e.g., "Make me not miss my flight") while the system determines how to realize them, though often with inherently indeterminate results. We discuss design opportunities for ShadAR and ethical concerns.

items.title: Shared leadership and ai-enabled contingency planning in Ukrainian firms during the 2022–2025 war
items.abstract: The full-scale invasion of Ukraine by the Russian Federation, which began in February 2022, caused acute and long-term disruptions in the activities of Ukrainian companies, forcing them to quickly rebuild their organizational structures, decision-making mechanisms, and planning practices. This article offers a conceptual and analytical explanation of how wartime conditions accelerated the transition from centralised management measures to cross-functional crisis teams, shared leadership mechanisms and emerging learning operating models. This study is based on secondary data analysis and illustrative case studies, rather than original empirical research. It combines business survey data, institutional and corporate reports, and academic literature. On this basis, the article outlines an organizational trajectory from centralization to distributed cross-functional decision-making and beyond to what this study defines as a learning operating model. The article also highlights that AI-enabled practices (including situational dashboards, scenario modeling, demand forecasting, and knowledge management) supported by generative AI can accelerate collective situational awareness in wartime. However, role overload and coordination burdens can also increase in the absence of clarity of purpose. Thus, shared leadership in the study is viewed as potentially “a dual-effect organizational mechanism”. The conclusions outline the implications for Ukrainian business practices and compare the identified trajectories of organizational response of Ukrainian companies with future constraints associated with the European model of AI governance. This paper addresses a gap in the literature by establishing a link among shared leadership, contingency planning, and AI-based situational analysis in the specific context of business resilience in wartime. And its practical contribution is to identify organizational conditions under which AI tools can support distributed decision making without increasing coordination overhead.

items.abstract: Due to their complex and multifaceted character, liver diseases represent a huge global health burden and contribute considerably to morbidity and mortality globally. Although the liver is essential for detoxification, protein synthesis, metabolic equilibrium, and biochemical regulation, it is extremely vulnerable to damage due to ongoing exposure to chemicals, medications, and infections. Hepatocellular carcinoma, alcoholic liver disease, fibrosis, cirrhosis, viral hepatitis, metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), and cirrhosis are among the liver diseases that frequently proceed asymptomatically and are identified at advanced stages, which limits the effectiveness of treatment. Interconnected processes including oxidative stress, mitochondrial dysfunction, inflammation, apoptosis, fibrosis, and immunological dysregulation are involved in the pathogenesis of liver injury. The main goals of conventional therapy approaches, such as liver transplantation, medication, and lifestyle changes, are to control symptoms and halt the course of the disease. However, they are not very effective at correcting extensive liver damage and may have negative side effects. Emerging hepatoprotective treatments that target several molecular pathways have been made possible by recent developments. Targeted pharmacological medicines (such as PPAR, FXR, and thyroid hormone receptor-β agonists), natural bioactive substances, drug delivery methods based on nanotechnology, gene and RNA-based therapies, stem cell-based regenerative techniques, immunotherapy, and gut microbiome modification are some of these. When assessing these treatments, experimental models such as those caused by CCl₄, paracetamol, alcohol, and diet-induced liver impairment are crucial. Furthermore, despite ongoing obstacles like a lack of trustworthy biomarkers, translational gaps, high prices, and regulatory restrictions, clinical trials and translational research are crucial for confirming their safety and efficacy. In order to improve therapeutic outcomes, future hepatoprotective techniques will prioritize multi-targeted approaches, personalized medicine, and the integration of omics technology and artificial intelligence. Despite tremendous advancements, more study and interdisciplinary cooperation are needed to get past current obstacles and provide medicines that are accessible, safe, and effective. All things considered, new hepatoprotective treatments have great potential to improve liver regeneration, restore hepatic function, and lower the prevalence of liver illnesses worldwide.

items.title: Simulation Environment Generation Using a Persona-aware LLM
items.abstract: Collecting diverse real-world data for AI model training is often costly, time-consuming, and constrained by safety and experimental conditions, making simulation environments an important alternative for data collection. However, existing methods for generating simulation environments often rely on predefined asset libraries and provide limited support for integrating user-specific personas. This paper proposes a persona-aware pipeline for generating 3D desk simulation environments based on a user persona defined by an occupation and Big Five personality traits. Given the input persona, an LLM generates structured scene layout information and an image generation model produces a synthetic desk image, followed by library-free 3D asset reconstruction using SAM 2 for object segmentation and SAM 3D for object-level 3D reconstruction. The assets are then rendered in Isaac Sim using grid mapping and scene graph-based spatial relationships. Experimental results show that persona variables produce interpretable changes in object composition and workspace atmosphere. Qualitative rendering results further show that the proposed pipeline can transfer the layout structure of a target image into a simulation environment, demonstrating its potential for generating diverse and controllable persona-aware simulation environments.

items.title: SkillNEO: Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization of Agent Skills
items.abstract: Agent skills turn procedural knowledge into reusable artifacts, allowing LLM agents to accumulate and refine expertise through experience. Building on this, skill evolution iteratively improves skills using execution feedback. However, improvement may require several interdependent edits, so low-reward versions can still be worth developing. Requiring immediate reward gains can discard useful partial repairs before their benefits emerge. Non-elitist evolution allows new versions to receive further edits despite scoring below earlier ones. For agent skills, this calls for evidence of what to preserve and repair next. We introduce SkillNEO (Non-Elitist Evolutionary Optimization for Agent Skills), which separately selects a version to use and versions to keep improving. Comparing how related versions perform the same task reveals working steps to preserve and remaining failures to fix. It can also revisit and revise earlier versions using later evidence. Across 86 SkillsBench tasks in eight domains, including software engineering and office work, SkillNEO raises GPT-5.4 Mini's average reward from 49.1% to 66.4%, within GPT-5.5 and GPT-5.6 Luna's original-skill range. Mini executes tasks, proposes revisions, and edits skills; final evaluation uses the same task instances. Gains span all eight domains. The same skills improve stronger models without further editing. On the 41 tasks with modified skills, reuse improves Luna by 10.5 percentage points and places GPT-5.5 10.6 points above its published original-skill reference. Execution records show these skills can benefit stronger models even when Mini still fails some task requirements. Search histories also show lower-scoring versions leading to skills ultimately selected for use. Together, these findings show that skill evolution can turn a weaker model's partial progress into reusable procedural knowledge for improving more capable agents.

items.title: Smart Crop Advisory System
items.abstract: The Smart Crop Advisory System is a web-based agricultural decision-support platform that uses Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) technologies to assist farmers in making informed farming decisions. Traditional agriculture faces several challenges, including unsuitable crop selection, unpredictable weather conditions, crop diseases, and fluctuations in market prices. The proposed system integrates essential agricultural services, including crop recommendation, weather forecasting, crop disease detection, agricultural market price information, and an AI-based multilingual voice assistant. It also provides farmer profile management, crop price trend analysis, and rainfall trend visualization through an interactive dashboard. The crop recommendation module helps farmers identify suitable crops based on relevant agricultural parameters, while the disease detection module supports the identification of potential crop diseases. Weather and market information help farmers plan agricultural activities and make informed selling decisions. The multilingual voice assistant aims to improve accessibility by enabling farmers to interact with the system through voice-based communication. Overall, the Smart Crop Advisory System aims to improve access to agricultural information, support effective decision-making, promote efficient resource utilization, and encourage sustainable farming practices. items.title: Social Media Fatigue and Depressive Symptoms Among Chinese University Students: Artificial Intelligence Anxiety as a Statistical Mediator and Subjective Socioeconomic Status as a Moderator
items.abstract: As social media and artificial intelligence (AI) become increasingly embedded in university students’ learning and daily lives, fatigue arising from established digital platforms and anxiety surrounding emerging AI may constitute interrelated forms of technology-related distress. However, how these experiences are jointly associated with depressive symptoms, and whether these associations vary by subjective socioeconomic status (SSES), remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on conservation of resources theory and research on status maintenance, this cross-sectional study examined AI anxiety as a statistical mediator of the association between social media fatigue and depressive symptoms and further tested whether SSES moderated the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms. Survey data from 1108 Chinese university students were analyzed using regression models with heteroscedasticity-consistent type 3 (HC3) robust standard errors and percentile-bootstrap confidence intervals. Social media fatigue was positively associated with AI anxiety, which in turn was positively associated with depressive symptoms, yielding a significant statistical indirect association. As SSES increased, the association between AI anxiety and depressive symptoms became stronger, and the corresponding conditional indirect association also increased. Overall, these findings suggest that understanding university students’ digital mental health requires attention to both distress arising across different technological environments and the subjective social positions from which these experiences are evaluated, offering a more context-sensitive perspective on how established and emerging forms of digital stress may be jointly associated with psychological well-being.

items.title: SoK: Grading Open-Text Legal Answers, from Law School Exams to Trustworthy Rubric Judges
items.abstract: Law students are examined through open-text answers: case solutions, essays and memos that apply the law to a set of facts. Such answers are expensive to grade, human graders disagree widely on them, and large language models (LLMs) now offer to grade them at scale, both in teaching and in the benchmarks that test legal AI. This paper systematizes how open-text legal answers can be evaluated. We derive eight desiderata from educational measurement and from the law that governs exams, among them validity, reliability, reasons, credit for defensible alternative solutions, robustness to gaming and human oversight. We then compare eight evaluation paradigms against them, from unstructured human grading to LLM judges with instance-specific rubrics and pairwise comparison. Three findings stand out. A rubric written for the task is the strongest lever for agreement between an LLM judge and human graders, but the reported figures answer different questions and rarely come with the human agreement they must be read against. The central validation gap lies where examination law is most demanding: defensible alternative solutions, follow-on errors, and the examiner's correction of model judgments. And rubric-centred grading is the most auditable family, because it makes the standard, its application and the final decision checkable. From this we derive the trustworthy rubric judge: an instance rubric that credits arguments and alternative paths,evidence checked in code, probes, repeated runs, calibration against independent human grades,logging, and an examiner who reads every script. We state what each safeguard rests on, what remains to be tested, and the uses the evidence supports today.

items.title: Sovereign OS v200 - Consolidated Architecture for Whole System Organisational Diagnostics
items.abstract: Sovereign OS v200 formalises a behavioural‑systems organisational diagnostic architecture capable of reading modern organisations as multi‑layer, multi‑domain, multi‑reality ecosystems. Building on the emergence of human–AI co‑processing documented in the Sovereign Cognition whitepaper, v200 integrates behavioural insight, cognitive altitude, and long‑context reasoning to produce a unified diagnostic model that neither human practitioners nor AI systems could generate independently. The architecture provides whole‑system organisational clarity by distinguishing between formal, informal, stated, lived, and emerging realities while tracing behavioural drift across cultural, operational, financial, compliance, strategic, and technical domains. v200 introduces consolidated diagnostic artefacts—including Whole‑System Maps, Coherence Frames, Integration Maps, Stability Indices, and Reality Alignment Frames—that detect instability long before traditional data sources reveal symptoms. Designed for complex, politically sensitive, multi‑stakeholder, and legacy‑constrained environments, Sovereign OS v200 establishes a new cognitive discipline for organisational diagnostics. It demonstrates how human–AI co‑processing can stabilise ecosystems, align realities, and support altitude‑based consulting across modern organisational landscapes.

items.title: Sparse Autoencoders Are a Shared Coordinate System for Symbolic Matching
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) hold broad knowledge in one set of weights, but lack interpretability and trustworthy reasoning, especially in high-stakes use cases. A neuro-symbolic model, with its interpretable architecture and System 2 reasoning capacity, is a promising alternative if built at the scale of LLMs; however, its symbolic backbone is usually constructed with human effort, so existing neuro-symbolic models are bottlenecked by the scope of the symbol component and usually domain-specific. A data-driven method could instead build a larger symbolic system by aligning and merging existing ones. We target its first, foundational step: matching units across these heterogeneous systems. Our method, SAE-IDF, encodes a symbol in its native context into a sparse code with a sparse autoencoder (SAE), re-weights each dimension by its rarity and matches across systems. On 12 tasks across 6 kinds of symbolic system, SAE-IDF outperforms the same LLM's dense baseline on all tasks with Gemma-2-9B and all but one with Llama-3.1-8B, by up to 45 points, consistently across SAE layers and configurations. SAE-IDF is also interpretable: every dimension of the sparse code has a human-readable meaning, so each match decomposes into named concepts (features). Our work paves the way to a universal symbolic backbone.

items.abstract: This article examines the role of psychological resilience and emotional self- regulation in enhancing athletes’ competitive performance. In sporting environments characterized by psychological pressure, pre-competition anxiety, unexpected setbacks, and high performance expectations, the ability to maintain psychological balance becomes particularly important. The article explores psychological resilience in relation to adapting to challenging situations, recovering from defeat, and sustaining intrinsic motivation. It also discusses the contribution of emotional self-regulation to attentional control, the management of impulsive reactions, and effective decision-making during competitions. Particular emphasis is placed on approaches to strengthening athletes’ psychological stability through specialized training exercises, individualized psychological support, and the development of self-regulation skills. These approaches may help improve athletes’ psychological preparedness and enable them to demonstrate their abilities more effectively under competitive conditions.

items.title: Statistical Inference in Reinforcement Learning: A Selective Survey
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is concerned with how intelligence agents take actions in a given environment to maximize the cumulative reward they receive. In healthcare, applying RL algorithms could assist patients in improving their health status. In ride-sharing platforms, applying RL algorithms could increase drivers’ income and customer satisfaction. For large language models, applying RL algorithms could align their outputs with human preferences. Over the past decade, RL has been arguably one of the most vibrant research frontiers in machine learning. Nevertheless, statistics as a field, as opposed to computer science, has only recently begun to engage with RL both in depth and in breadth. This chapter presents a selective review of statistical inferential tools for RL, covering both hypothesis testing and confidence interval construction. Our goal is to highlight the value of statistical inference in RL for both the statistics and machine learning communities, and to promote the broader application of classical statistical inference tools in this vibrant area of research.

items.title: Strategi Membangun Talenta Berbasis AI untuk Meningkatkan Kompetensi dan Daya Saing Sumber Daya Manusia Digital
items.abstract: Digital transformation has changed the way organizations manage human resources, particularly in identifying, developing, placing, and retaining talent. The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in talent management enables organizations to utilize data to support recruitment, competency mapping, employee development, career planning, performance evaluation, and talent retention. This article aims to analyze strategies for building AI-based talent by reviewing eight articles related to artificial intelligence, talent management, human resource development, talent acquisition, and data integration. This study uses a literature review approach by comparing the findings, research focuses, methods, benefits, and challenges discussed in the selected sources. The literature indicates that AI can support organizations in identifying talent and employee potential, analyzing competency gaps, providing personalized learning programs, supporting career development, and predicting employee turnover risks. However, AI implementation also presents challenges, including algorithmic bias, data quality limitations, lack of transparency, privacy concerns, organizational readiness, and the need for digital competencies. Therefore, an AI-based talent development strategy should integrate technology, data quality, organizational readiness, leadership, employee development, and ethical governance. AI should complement human judgment rather than replace the human role in talent management. This collaboration can improve talent management while maintaining contextual, relational, and ethical considerations.

items.title: Strategic Management in AI-Orchestrated Organizations: A Dynamic Capabilities Perspective
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing organizational strategy, decision-making, resource allocation, and operational coordination. As AI moves from task automation and analytical support toward generative systems and intelligent agents, its role is expanding across organizational functions. AI-orchestrated organizations integrate AI capabilities with human expertise to support information analysis, opportunity identification, decision support, workflow coordination, and learning. This creates opportunities for greater strategic responsiveness, while also raising issues of decision authority, accountability, governance, and organizational control. This study examines AI orchestration through a dynamic capabilities perspective and develops a conceptual framework linking AI-enabled sensing, strategic seizing, resource reconfiguration, human–AI coordination, governance, and continuous learning. The framework positions AI as an enabling organizational capability rather than an isolated technological resource and emphasizes the interaction between technological capabilities, human judgement, organizational resources, and governance. It further explains how these elements can support strategic responsiveness, organizational agility, and continuous adaptation as organizations respond to changing environments. The study develops seven conceptual propositions to provide a structured basis for future empirical examination of AI-orchestrated strategic management.

items.title: StreamErase: Towards Ultra-Fast Streaming Video Erasing
items.abstract: Current video object removal methods suffer from prohibitive latency (minutes per video) and non-causal processing that prevents real-time interaction. We present StreamErase, enabling sub-second latency with up to 26 FPS streaming generation on a single GPU. Our approach first augments a text-to-video model with mask input to generate high-quality videos that erase target objects and synthesize coherent backgrounds, but does not perform inference on the fly. As such, we progressively transfer the erasing capability from a powerful bidirectional foundation model to an efficient unidirectional streaming eraser, enabling long-horizon erasing without sacrificing visual fidelity. Several key challenges arise when generating videos over long, potentially infinite horizons: (1) bridging the domain gap from training on finite length and extrapolating to long horizons, (2) sustaining high quality by preventing error accumulation, and (3) maintaining fast inference, without increasing computational cost as the context grows. To address these challenges, we carefully designed sliding-window causal attention with attention sinks. By incorporating self-rollout with attention sinks and KV cache rolling during training, we simulate inference-time extrapolations with a fixed context window, enabling constant-speed generation of arbitrarily long videos. Finally, we establish a dedicated benchmark, LongErase, for streaming long-video object removal. Our model achieves strong performance compared to existing video object erasing models and generalizes well to real-world video scenarios, uniquely enabling infinite-length streaming. With StreamErase, users can input a mask and see the erasing results unfold in real-time, delivering a truly interactive experience.

items.title: Strengthening Perioperative Patient Safety Through Non-Technical Skills Training Among Surgical Teams at Hakim Gezaw Teaching Hospital, Ethiopia
items.abstract: Background: Non-technical skills such as communication, teamwork, situational awareness, decision-making, adaptability, task management and leadership are important for patient safety during surgery. Evidence evaluating context-adapted multidisciplinary interventions and their relationship with patient-level safety outcomes remains limited in low- and middle-income countries, including Ethiopia. Aim: To assess changes in non-technical skills following context-adapted training and examine selected perioperative patient safety outcomes at Hakim Gezaw Teaching Hospital, Ethiopia. Methods: A mixed-methods quasi-experimental pre–post study included 24 multidisciplinary operating-room professionals and 672 adult surgical patients. Staff non-technical skills were assessed before training, immediately afterwards and at one month using an eight-item, five-point Likert-scale instrument informed by NOTSS, ANTS and SPLINTS frameworks. Linear mixed-effects models assessed changes in staff scores. Patient outcomes were compared between 336 pre-intervention and 336 post-intervention patients. Focus group discussions were analysed thematically and integrated with quantitative findings. Results: Mean overall non-technical skills scores rose from 3.36 ± 0.37 at baseline to 3.82 ± 0.34 immediately after training and 4.04 ± 0.61 at one month. Adjusted mean differences versus baseline were 0.464 (95% CI 0.161–0.766) immediately after training and 0.679 (95% CI 0.373–0.985) at one month. Situational awareness, adaptability and task management showed significant improvement. The post-intervention period was associated with fewer adverse events, care delays and communication-related safety events, alongside higher patient satisfaction. Qualitative findings described improvements in teamwork, communication, shared awareness, coordination and speaking up. Conclusion: Context-adapted training was associated with improved team non-technical skills, maintained at one month. Concurrent improvements in patient outcomes cannot be attributed causally to the intervention because the study had no control group. Routine integration, refresher training and supportive leadership may help sustain improvements. Keywords: Non-technical skills; Patient safety; Teamwork; Communication; Operating room; Ethiopia.

items.title: Students as change agents for societal challenges –
items.abstract: In 2025, the Centre for Interprofessional Workplace Learning (TVEPS) co-designed a Blended Intensive Programme (BIP) with partners from Denmark, Sweden, and Norway as part of a NordPlus project. The aim was for students from different disciplines and countries to become agents of change for grand societal challenges through collaboration on wicked problems in a workshop with representatives from municipalities and educational institutions. Exploring real-life wicked problems without straightforward solutions can enable students, municipalities, and scientific staff to create social, environmental, and economic value and to contribute to the fulfilment of the UN Sustainable Development Goals, including the provision of ethical and responsible healthcare services. The workshop comprised two parts: an online week and a one-week on-site challenge workshop at Chalmers University of Technology. Stockholm, Sweden. The students were introduced to grand societal challenges from the municipalities of Øygarden (Norway), Kolding (Denmark), and Aarhus (Denmark). Their task was to explore wicked problems in interprofessional teams comprising students from health, social care, engineering, design, and entrepreneurship disciplines, using an innovation process to identify sustainable opportunities and hypotheses that could later be investigated, developed, and implemented in collaboration with the municipalities. During the challenge workshop, the student teams engaged in close dialogue with municipal representatives, experts in municipal economics, and facilitators from the educational institutions. Educational institutions derived significant benefits from the interprofessional, cross-sectoral, Nordic teaching format. Students gained valuable insight through reflection and close collaboration, developing innovative perspectives, potential opportunities, and hypotheses related to the societal challenges presented. These can be further developed and implemented to benefit the participating municipalities, whose representatives received input of potentially high societal value.

items.title: Students’ Lived Experiences on the Use of Artificial Intelligence Tools in Learning Social Studies
items.abstract: This study explored the lived experiences of Grade 12 Humanities and Social Sciences (HUMSS) students in using Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools for learning Social Studies in Malapatan III District, Schools Division of Sarangani, Philippines. Anchored in Moustakas’ Transcendental Phenomenology, Davis’ Technology Acceptance Model, and Zimmerman’s Self-Regulated Learning Theory, the study employed a qualitative phenomenological research design. Nine Grade 12 HUMSS students from three public secondary schools participated in in-depth interviews, while three Social Studies teachers participated in a focus group discussion for data triangulation. Participants were selected through purposive sampling, and data were gathered using a validated semi-structured interview guide and analyzed thematically. The findings identified twelve emerging themes encompassing students’ lived experiences, the contexts shaping AI-supported learning, and their perspectives on future AI integration. Participants perceived AI as a valuable learning resource that improved conceptual understanding, academic productivity, confidence, classroom engagement, and emotional well-being. However, excessive dependence, reduced independent thinking, information accuracy, and academic integrity emerged as significant concerns. Students emphasized the importance of responsible AI use, critical evaluation, and continued teacher guidance. The study recommends strengthening AI literacy, ethical practices, and teacher capacity building through the proposed Responsible Artificial Intelligence Integration and Learning Empowerment Program (RAILEP). The findings primarily support Sustainable Development Goal 4 (Quality Education) by promoting responsible, inclusive, and learner-centered technology integration. The study contributes to educational and institutional sustainability by informing school-based guidelines and instructional practices that balance technological innovation with academic integrity, learner autonomy, and meaningful human interaction.

items.title: Study on how Al can reduce financial fraud among women
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in mitigating online financial fraud among women, analyzing survey data from 75 respondents. The demographic profile is heavily skewed toward younger, digital-native generations, with 92% of respondents aged 18–35 and nearly half (46.7%) identifying as students. This sample exhibits high digital integration, with 73.3% utilizing digital payment applications daily. Concurrently, risk exposure is pervasive: 89.3% are aware of online cybercrimes, and 74.7% have direct or secondary experience with financial scams—predominantly fake loan apps, UPI fraud, and OTP scams. Consequently, 69.3% express deep anxiety regarding transaction safety. To counteract these threats, respondents strongly endorse technological intervention. General AI literacy is high at 70.7%, and 68% recognize AI’s current application in banking security. Optimism regarding its efficacy is robust: 70.7% believe AI can significantly reduce financial fraud targeting women, primarily because 74.7% trust it to detect threats faster than human operators. To establish a sense of security, users demand proactive, real-time defenses rather than passive analysis, heavily prioritizing instant fraud alerts (37.3%), background transaction monitoring, and automated transaction blocking. Ultimately, 72% of respondents demand that banking institutions escalate AI security integration. However, the data highlights that technology alone is insufficient; an overwhelming 78.7% emphasize that robust AI deployment must be paired with comprehensive financial literacy and grassroots cybersecurity awareness campaigns. This dual strategy of advanced technological defense and target user education is deemed essential to safely empower women within the digital economy.

items.title: Sufficient and necessary conditions in the adoption of generative artificial intelligence by entrepreneurs: findings in Spain
items.abstract: Purpose This study assesses the use of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) among entrepreneurs in Spain, examining both sufficient and necessary conditions for different levels of use. Design/methodology/approach The study uses survey data from the Centro de Investigaciones Sociológicas. Ordered logistic regression is applied to identify sufficient conditions, while Necessary Condition Analysis is used to detect bottlenecks for higher levels of GenAI use. Findings Knowledge of GenAI and perceived economic usefulness are the main predictors of more intensive use. However, the NCA shows that technological optimism and the absence of very high scepticism operate as necessary conditions, especially at regular levels of use. Research limitations/implications The assessment relies on cross-sectional, self-reported data from Spanish self-employed workers. Future research should distinguish between different entrepreneurial profiles and types of GenAI use. The analytical framework may be applicable across different contexts, although the specific associations and bottleneck thresholds observed here should be validated through cross-country research. Practical implications Support policies should combine awareness-raising, applied training, and practical guidance on how GenAI can generate value in entrepreneurial activity. Social implications The findings suggest that responsible GenAI adoption among entrepreneurs requires not only favourable attitudes towards technology but also knowledge, perceived usefulness, and clear guidance on its business applications. Originality/value The study contributes by combining sufficiency and necessity logics to explain actual GenAI use among entrepreneurs, rather than focussing only on behavioural intention, while indicating that technology-readiness dispositions and GenAI-specific behavioural factors may fulfil distinct roles at different levels of use. By distinguishing probabilistic drivers from necessary bottlenecks, the study provides a more complete account of entrepreneurial GenAI adoption and generates more actionable implications for training and policies aimed at increasing effective use.

items.title: Support and fracture: understanding sociotechnical imaginaries in Chinese grassroots’ AI governance frames
items.abstract: This study examines how Chinese grassroots publics construct and contest sociotechnical imaginaries (SIs) of AI governance. Drawing on six online focus groups with 30 non-expert participants, we integrate SIs with Technological Frame to explore three dimensions of AI imaginaries: social representations, governance mechanisms, and future trajectories. Findings reveal a marked divergence between instrumentalist and humanistic imaginaries, generating competing narratives at the intersection of technological development and governance. However, these imaginaries are constrained by structural power asymmetries that limit grassroots publics’ capacities to envision future technological directions. This constraint gives rise to SIs fracture, a loss of imaginative agency where idealized futures feel inaccessible. As a result, individuals retreat from governance discourse, perceiving AI development as a vehicle for disempowering control. This study thus highlights how structural power asymmetries undermine public imaginaries and pose critical risks to inclusive technological futures.

items.title: Synthetic Hate Speech Data Underrepresents Minority Groups
items.abstract: The use of synthetic data is becoming increasingly widespread in a variety of applications. For hate speech detection, synthetic data offers the chance to overcome limitations of existing models and datasets, such as data scarcity, negative psychological impact on annotators, and privacy issues. However, previous work on the topic has only focused on evaluating synthetic datasets extrinsically, by measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic texts. In this work, in addition to measuring the performance of models trained on synthetic data in cross-distribution setups, we carry out a qualitative analysis, aiming at assessing how closely synthetic data can mimic authentic user-generated and human-annotated data. We focus in particular on possible issues related to (under)representation of specific minority groups as targets of hate in synthetic data. To do this, we augment an existing English hate speech dataset by paraphrasing the original gold data using three large language models, and then evaluate the synthetic data both quantitatively, including testing out-of-distribution model generalization, and qualitatively, examining the realism of synthetic texts, their hate speech content, and whether they represent the same identity groups as the original data. We pair this analysis with a detailed breakdown, for each demographic characteristic, of how the synthetic data creation process affects the representation of each specific type of identity, which is the main contribution of our work. We find that, while the performance of models trained on synthetic data is promising, these texts are easily identified as written by an LLM by humans, hate speech labels are not necessarily preserved, and the paraphrasing process tends to erase representation of minority groups and intersectional identities, affecting certain demographics more than others.

items.title: Tactile-Guided Robot Learning: From Representation Learning to Foundation Models
items.abstract: Tactile sensing is becoming central to robust, adaptive, and dexterous robotic manipulation. Beyond its traditional role in contact detection and reactive control, touch is increasingly used to learn transferable representations, condition manipulation policies, and support embodied physical reasoning. Yet existing surveys largely emphasize tactile hardware and perception, leaving the rapid shift toward learning-based tactile manipulation insufficiently synthesized. This paper reviews tactile-guided skill learning from a learning-centric perspective, organized by the functional role of touch across the learning and control pipeline. We examine tactile representation and policy learning, tactile foundation models, predictive and adaptive control, and generalization across objects, tasks, sensors, embodiments, and simulation-to-real transfer. Across these directions, we identify common design principles and remaining challenges in learning transferable physical representations, integrating semantic reasoning with contact-level control, and scaling tactile learning across heterogeneous data and hardware. Finally, we outline emerging directions toward tactile foundation and world models that can predict, reason about, and adapt physical interactions. Together, this review characterizes the transition of touch from a task-specific feedback signal toward a core modality for general-purpose embodied intelligence. An accompanying database of the reviewed literature and associated resources is available at https://sites.google.com/view/touch-in-robot-learning-review.

items.title: Teacher Educators' Readiness for Integrating Artificial Intelligence into Classroom Teaching: A Case Study
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing educational practices, introducing innovative approaches to teaching, learning, assessment, and classroom management. The successful implementation of AI in educational institutions largely depends on the preparation and acceptance of teachers, especially teacher trainers, who play a key role in training future teachers. This study examines the perceptions, perceptions, and readiness of bachelor's degree recipients in education. University teacher on the integration of artificial intelligence into school education. A descriptive survey design was used to collect data from 25 randomly selected undergraduate faculty members. Universities in Indore city were surveyed through a structured questionnaire. The collected data were analysed using percentage analysis. The results showed that the majority of participants had a positive view of AI and recognized its potential to improve teaching effectiveness, support personalized learning, and reduce administrative burden on teachers. However, concerns related to ethical concerns, data privacy, inadequate training, and inadequate organizational infrastructure continue to impact teachers' readiness to adopt AI. The study recommends integrating an AI culture into teacher preparation programs, strengthening digital infrastructure, and organizing regular professional development efforts to effectively and responsibly integrate AI into educational environments. items.title: Teaching AI, teaching bias: addressing gender inequality in public health education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes healthcare, public health and health professions education. However, predictive and generative systems can reproduce or amplify longstanding inequalities embedded in data, institutions and established knowledge structures. Public health education therefore needs to connect technical approaches to identifying and mitigating algorithmic bias with their broader social, population health and institutional contexts. This conceptual article presents the sociotechnical Bias literacy for public health education framework (SBL-PHE), developed through a theory-informed conceptual synthesis drawing on conceptual framework analysis. A focused supplementary literature search in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, ERIC and the ACM digital library was conducted to examine and refine its theoretical foundations. An evidence-informed composite case of AI-supported cardiovascular risk assessment traces algorithmic gender bias from knowledge production and data representation through modeling and implementation to monitoring. The framework comprises five interconnected competency dimensions concerned with recognizing, explaining, evaluating, addressing and reflecting on algorithmic bias. For master’s-level public health education, these dimensions are linked to learning objectives, learning activities, assessment methods and a prospective evaluation strategy. Sociotechnical Bias literacy is proposed as a foundational competency for public health professionals who use or interpret AI. Sociotechnical fluency describes an advanced, role-dependent capability, particularly for responsibilities in implementation, evaluation, translation and governance. SBL-PHE provides a theoretically grounded framework for integrating technical understanding, health equity, professional judgment and institutional responsibility into public health education. The framework and its proposed educational application have not yet been empirically validated.

items.title: Teaching computational toxicology as new approach methodologies in the era of next-generation risk assessment
items.abstract: The global initiative toward non-animal chemical testing methods has recently gained significant momentum, requiring developing new approach methodologies (NAMs) as transformative solutions for next-generation risk assessment (NGRA). NAMs refer to any in chemico, in silico , and in vitro technology, methodology, or combination that do not rely on animals. A range of computational toxicology methods are becoming critical components within the NGRA framework across multiple testing tiers. These approaches are needed to support hazard characterization and prioritization for further testing, calculate points of departure, identify modes of action, and bridge the data gaps between in vitro assays and in vivo exposures as well as apical health endpoints. The core technologies of computational toxicology include (i) quantitative structure activity relationship, (ii) benchmark dose modeling, (iii) bioinformatic analysis of omics data, (iv) physiologically based kinetic modeling, (v) quantitative adverse outcome pathway modeling, (vi) molecular docking and dynamics, and (vii) more recently, machine learning and artificial intelligence tools. The NAM community, in academia, industry, and regulatory agencies, are facing increasing demand for training current and future professionals to master these skills. In this article, we described our perspective, experiences, and challenges in disseminating these computational toxicology techniques. Unlike established disciplines, the curriculum of computational toxicology and associated software tools are constantly evolving, requiring instructors to adapt in a timely manner. Challenges abound, we are embraced with an unprecedented opportunity that educating next-generation toxicologists is a critical effort of this revolutionary movement of chemical toxicity testing and safety assessment.

items.title: Team signal detection theory: objective team performance measurement using simulation telemetry
items.abstract: Current methods for evaluating team performance rely primarily on simple outcome measures and subjective ratings, which offer limited insight into the decision processes driving performance. This study extends signal detection theory (SDT) to teams, deriving sensitivity (d′) and response bias (c) from simulation telemetry. Twenty three-person teams completed five virtual reality tasks varying in interdependence and time pressure while self-reported workload, conventional and SDT metrics, and verbal communication were collected. Team-level sensitivity distinguished conditions that conventional metrics did not. High time pressure reduced sensitivity relative to baseline before task scores declined, suggesting sensitivity may indicate early performance degradation. Response bias became more conservative under combined high interdependence and time pressure, reflecting team strategy shifts. SDT metrics correlated with workload, particularly team-task balancing demands (rs=−0.68 for d′). Together, sensitivity and bias characterise team performance more completely than accuracy alone by separating discriminative ability from decision strategy.

items.title: Technology readiness in maintenance: an Industry 4.0 case study in the Swedish sawmill sector with Industry 5.0 human-centric insights
items.abstract: Abstract The sawmill industry presents unique opportunities for adopting emerging technologies due to its capital-intensive operations and dependence on high reliability. However, despite increasing digitalization, there remains limited understanding of how maintenance organizations can assess and develop technology readiness, particularly with respect to organizational and human factors. Understanding these factors is important not only for operational efficiency but also for supporting the human-centric, sustainable, and resilient ambitions of Industry 5.0. This paper investigates the technology readiness of maintenance operations in a Swedish sawmill. The study is based on a qualitative case study involving 21 in-depth interviews and three workshops with personnel from the maintenance organization (technicians, engineers, coordinators, and managers) and related functions (production, operations development, health and safety, and management). Findings reveal that while the organization demonstrates strengths in technology adoption and operational structure, challenges remain in areas such as strategic integration, workforce competence, and data utilization. The study highlights that advancing technology utilization and work processes alone is insufficient for successful development of maintenance. Thus, the study emphasizes human-centric perspectives such as leadership visibility, shared responsibility, cross-functional communication, and long-term planning, are critical for achieving technology readiness. The study concludes that technology readiness in maintenance depends on the combined development of technological, organizational, and human capabilities. Maintenance can serve as a strategic entry point for this transformation, enabling improved sustainability, resilience, and safer operations. Further research is recommended to combine methods and explore how human-centric factors influence the successful adoption of smart technologies.

items.title: Technology-mediated emergence of a competing logic in a mature field: The case of Bitcoin
items.abstract: Emerging technologies, such as blockchain and artificial intelligence, are enabling new configurations of practices, roles, and meaning systems within mature fields that can disrupt institutionalized field arrangements and alter the centrality of institutional logics. Given the growing significance of this phenomenon, we aim to understand the constitutive role of technology's materiality in such processes. Through a historical processual analysis of Bitcoin, we propose a process model of disruptive institutional change, in which a challenger proto-institution emerges from the periphery and introduces a competing logic in a mature field. We identify four mechanisms underlying this process: inscription, field-anchoring, translation, and contestation. Our proposed framework highlights the dual role of the technology artifact: as a contra-institutional technology that carries a marginal conflicting logic into the mature field and, simultaneously, as a boundary object that remains interpretively flexible and affords agency to heterogeneous actors drawing on different institutional logics. We theorize that the marginal conflicting logic inscribed in the technology is instantiated and strengthened at the field level as diverse actors, drawing on different institutional logics, develop and adopt novel technology-based field practices. As a boundary object, the technology enables these distributed efforts by actors pursuing different goals. As a carrier of the marginal conflicting logic, it anchors the dispersed efforts to the strengthening of that logic and, consequently, toward its emergence as a competing logic in the field.

items.title: TEX-MEX: Similarity-Guided Temporal Contrastive Learning for Time Series
items.abstract: Contrastive learning for time series depends on deciding which pairs of inputs should be treated as similar and dissimilar. Because few augmentations reliably preserve meaning in time series, prior methods have relied on two disjoint notions of similarity between windows: structural similarity, which relates windows with similar morphology, and temporal similarity, which relates windows that occur close together in time. We introduce TEX-MEX, to our knowledge the first approach to unify the two into a single relationship. Given a random batch of windows drawn across the dataset, TEX-MEX uses the encoder to identify which windows are structurally similar or dissimilar to each other. It then pulls each window toward the temporally shifted versions of similar windows and pushes it away from those of dissimilar ones, learning what typically accompanies similar windows in time. Across PPG, EEG, ECG, accelerometry, and continuous glucose monitoring, TEX-MEX broadly achieves state-of-the-art performance against contrastive, reconstructive, JEPA-based, and modality-specific approaches, establishing it as a strong general SSL objective. We further train a 560K-parameter PPG foundation model that achieves state-of-the-art performance across a broad range of downstream benchmarks while being roughly 50x smaller than the next-best unimodally pretrained PPG foundation model in our evaluation. We will release this foundation model open-source and open-weight to the community to support future work and practical applications.

items.title: Text-Informed Training Data Filtering for Enhanced Virtual Flow Meter Performance
items.abstract: In sectors such as energy, aquaculture and chemical processing, the effectiveness of both mechanistic and data-driven models is frequently limited by poor-quality training data, which obscures underlying physical laws and degrades predictive accuracy. Such quality issues commonly manifest as anomalies in the dataset, ranging from sensor faults to process upsets and incorrect operator inputs. While traditional rule-based filtering can remove a subset of the anomalies, it is unable to leverage contextual information stored as unstructured text, such as engineer comments and operational logs that explain under what conditions the data was collected. We propose a text-informed data filtering method that leverages large language models (LLMs) to integrate unstructured operational data with tabular sensor data. The method consists of two steps: (1) contextual anomaly detection by reasoning over both data modalities, and (2) generation of a binary mask that is applied to filter the training dataset for model development. To investigate the potential benefit, a steady-state soft-sensor regression model, namely a virtual flow meter that estimates well flow rates, is used as the downstream evaluation target. Experiments on a synthetic oil and gas dataset show improved model performance compared to traditional rule-based filtering. Ablation studies show that textual operator comments can provide filtering-relevant signals beyond sensor data alone, with the multimodal approach reducing downstream MAPE from 7.1% to 5.4% relative to sensor-only filtering. This work demonstrates that integrating unstructured operational knowledge with sensor data through LLMs can improve data quality for industrial machine learning applications, offering a scalable alternative to manual data curation.
